parts.title: Part III · The baseline world, measured every way

chapters.title: Meta II · What the measurements say about open-ended evolution
How different are the agents?
chapters.note: Every brain of a world put into the same situations: how much of what an agent does comes from where it is, who it is and chance; how many kinds of behaviour live side by side, and whether they last.

chapters.title: Flow modules: the groups tokens stay in
chapters.note: The groups a token tends to stay inside (the map equation), in every world, set beside the same flow with every agent's partners dealt among its neighbours: B1's groups are its network's, B2's flow is pairs, and only B2's agents keep a partner longer than chance.

chapters.title: Lightning in every world
chapters.note: Loops of flow measured in every world the book has made: B1's flow goes round and B2's runs one way, decided by whether unused links lapse; the longest loop is as long as the world is wide.

parts.title: Part IV · One change at a time

chapters.title: How does a world's size follow its tokens?
Brains replaced by their average
chapters.note: A better control than decisions by chance (Chapter 41): every decision drawn at random from the distribution of that decision in the settled baseline worlds — first unconditionally, then given the agent's own tokens and connections. If a world of such agents looks like the baseline, what the brains add is their average, not what they respond to.

chapters.title: What keeps wealth spread?
chapters.note: No coalitions: allow_revolutions off, against the baseline runs of Chapter 10.

chapters.title: Meta III
chapters.note: Written once Chapters 41 to 44 are analysed.

chapters.title: How to tell a world that keeps evolving
Brains that see, and worlds that break
A world that cannot break
chapters.note: The rules of space: a newborn joins its parent and two of its neighbours; a death is mended; only redundant links lapse; a brain may choose only so many links; no handover. Space alone (no brains) and space under the game: the health bar of Chapter 46.

chapters.title: Who dies, and why
chapters.note: The rules of demography and the exploits they invite: children spent as missiles, a hoarding queen with half the tokens, worlds of one-token agents; the last token kept at home, a longest life, a smallest child, a home share.

chapters.title: Strategies written by hand
chapters.note: Is the evolved play the best there is? Strategies written by hand — a turtle that only defends, a raider, and a factory whose members pump tokens to their frontier — planted as a patch in evolved worlds, against a patch of the residents' own brains.

chapters.title: How big should a brain be?
chapters.note: Brain size in a world that cannot break: B2 with hidden layers of 8, 16, 32 and 16 + 16, judged by cross-time tournaments.

chapters.title: The switches the world was built with
chapters.note: The original algorithm's own switches, judged for open-ended evolution with the tournaments of Chapter 46: revolutions on and off, gifts, connections that must be used, estates shared by wealth — in B1 and in B2.

chapters.title: Another game
chapters.note: Two contests other than Colonel Blotto's, with no number in them: a lottery, in which every staked token is a ticket, and stakes pooled by genotype, in which agents with one brain fight as one side.

chapters.title: Alliances
chapters.note: Cooperation with a surplus: two neighbours that both want it are allied, and their stakes on a node count together. One alliance grows until it holds the whole world, and with it the fighting ends.

chapters.title: Rules without numbers
chapters.note: B2 has seven numbers in its rules. What each does, shown by taking them away: worlds that die out, and a world of one peaceful alliance that grows as a tree.

chapters.title: Gliders, and who helps whom
chapters.note: Patterns that outlast the agents in them, after Conway's Game of Life: puffers, gliders, blinkers and guns made of takeovers, and tokens that run downhill or go round. Then help, defined by the rules: a stake without which a neighbour would have lost its node.

chapters.title: Meta IV
chapters.note: What the engineering of Part V found: what makes a world that cannot break, what keeps evolution from going on, and the experiments that would show whether larger worlds go further.

chapters.title: Who inherits?
chapters.note: Three new rules for the estate of the dead — to the poorest, to the newborns, to their parents — in B1 and B2: estates that pay for births fill a world with more, poorer and more alike agents, and in B2 stop evolution; the safety net does little.

chapters.title: Brains mixed at birth, units that cost, an eye for raids on kin
chapters.note: Three more pilot ideas in B2: brains mixed from two parents at birth, brains whose every unit holds a token, an input for raids on one's own kind — and links that hold a token in a world without old age.

chapters.title: Mixed at birth: ten long worlds
chapters.note: Brains mixed at birth in ten worlds of B2 for 10,000 iterations: rich, because their agents put off having children, but only half of them healthy, since health follows a size that drifts; evolution goes on.

chapters.title: Links to strangers
chapters.note: Agents that can reach past their neighbours to propose a link — by a paid jump, a scout, or a free reach: they hardly pay for a search, and the free one finds friends of friends; the network grows denser, not wider, and every searching world evolves faster than B2.

chapters.title: Brains mixed at birth, with every other rule
chapters.note: Mixing combined with 23 other rules (batch Y): it keeps its riches with sixteen, loses them to the rules that pay for or replace births, raises diversity nearly everywhere, and evolution goes on with nearly every one.

chapters.title: Mixed at birth, with parents as mates
chapters.note: Experiment 19: if only an agent with a living child may be a mate, does a mixed world stop breeding itself to death? All ten worlds lived to 20,000 iterations and settled at about 2,000 agents, six in ten of them poor: the agents breed twice as eagerly, the worlds keep mixing's diversity and B2's network, and evolution goes on.

chapters.title: Eight switches at once
chapters.note: Eight of the book's switches thrown together on B2 in sixteen worlds (batch U, a fractional factorial design): every unused link lapsing is the strongest switch, the estate to the newborns fills a world, mixing raises diversity; pairs of switches act together, and several switches do far less among the sixteen than alone in B2. On B1 (batch V) few switches stand out against the pairs, and none makes its evolution go on.

chapters.title: Revolutions, with every other rule
chapters.note: B2 without revolutions together with each of 24 other rules (batch W): for nearly every rule nothing changes, as revolutions are rare in B2's kind of world; with brains mixed at birth, where they are common, they keep a world small and rich.

chapters.title: Handover, with every other rule
chapters.note: B2 with handover together with each of 23 other rules (batch X): it costs two marks of the health bar with nearly every rule, thinning the network into trees; it cancels mixing's riches; it unfolds a world a little, since parents pass their links on.

chapters.title: Gifts, with every other rule
chapters.note: B2 with gifts together with each of 21 other rules, and B1 with gifts (batch T): gifts move a few thousandths of the tokens a game, mostly to the poorer, and change little whatever else the rules are; they cost mixing some of its riches, and in B1 without revolutions they fill the world with the poor.

parts.title: Part VI · Towards a physics: space, scale and locality

chapters.title: Dimensions at scale
chapters.note: The measures of Chapter 24 on the worlds of 100,000 tokens (Chapter 60): does a world look three-dimensional only at middle scales, as causal dynamical triangulations look four-dimensional only at large ones? Ball growth and the spectral dimension as functions of scale, and the width of worlds from 3,200 to 409,600 tokens (Chapter 42).

chapters.title: Which properties have no scale?
chapters.note: The same quantities measured at many sizes and rescaled: do their distributions collapse onto one curve? Starts from the cuts of Chapter 42, whose share of a world has the same distribution at every size.

chapters.title: Local rules only
chapters.note: The three rules that reach across a world, each made local: a piece that separates lives on, the tokens of the dead go to their former neighbours, and every agent draws its random numbers from a stream of its own (Chapter 7).

chapters.title: How far does a difference travel?
chapters.note: Twin worlds that differ in one token at one agent: how fast the difference spreads and whether it grows or dies away — the light cone of Chapter 7, measured. Needs the local random numbers of Chapter 63.

chapters.title: A source and a sink
chapters.note: A world with a flow running through it: tokens that are spent when used and slowly renewed, or a few nodes that release tokens and a way for tokens to leave. What forms in the flow? (Chapter 7; research/Research.md §4.3.)

chapters.title: Particles
chapters.note: Patterns that persist while what carries them changes: tokens bound in loops, groups that outlast their members, local beats in the flow of tokens (Chapter 7).

chapters.title: One agent in a sea of average agents
chapters.note: A large world of agents that decide as the average evolved agent does (Chapter 43), and in it a single agent, or a small group, with a brain of its own: can it draw tokens from the sea without exhausting it or being cut off, can its line invade, can a group hold together? Invasion analysis and a reservoir, in one experiment.

chapters.title: Meta V
chapters.note: What the measurements say about space, scale and matter, written once Chapters 60 to 67 are analysed.

chapters.title: What folds a world
chapters.note: Chapter 24's rulers on B2 and every world since: B2 is nearly a small world; every B2 world starts as a space and folds when its first generation dies, because death with mending folds it; without old age or mending, or with lapsing links, worlds keep their room, and the estates to the newborns or the parents make a space of about three dimensions.

chapters.title: Five mixed worlds, fifty thousand iterations
chapters.note: The five worlds of Experiment 17 that met every mark, played on to 50,000 iterations: three died out, the two that lived grew larger and poorer, and evolution faded — a mixed world is mortal.

chapters.title: The candidates, played on
chapters.note: Meta X's candidates — worlds that met every mark with diverse agents at iteration 1,000 — played on to 10,000: which held, which fell back, which died out on the way. Experiment 20 plays the two unfinished ones of engine rules in the lab.

chapters.title: Five more seeds for the rules that held
chapters.note: Experiment 21: the rules whose candidate held over 10,000 iterations — mixing with a fast change of brains, with no random inputs, with no revolutions — in five new worlds each, beside plain mixing in the same seeds.

chapters.title: Meta VI · Every world side by side
chapters.note: Every simulation made so far in one table: two clouds of worlds, what the settings decide and what the seed does, and which measure has been taken of which world.

chapters.title: Meta VII · Where tokens go
chapters.note: What the book knows about where tokens go: the budget of a game, the even split and where tokens come to rest, the downhill drain, how little goes round beyond chance, the groups tokens stay in, and the estate of the dead.

chapters.title: Meta VIII · Who helps whom
chapters.note: Every chapter that looked for cooperation, side by side: where help exists, why so little, what was tried to make it pay, and what would have to change.

chapters.title: Meta IX · How alike the agents are
chapters.note: Genotypes, brains and behaviour: how much of the variety of a world is real, what makes agents alike (one rule is enough: every unused link lapses), and what it would take for many kinds to evolve.

chapters.title: Meta X · Healthy and rich
chapters.note: Every world against the author's picture of one that might keep evolving: a decentralised, resilient, nearly three-dimensional network and agents that differ in almost everything. B1's worlds are rich but fragile, B2's healthy but poor; brains mixed at birth come closest.

chapters.title: Meta XI · What holds a world's size
chapters.note: Why B2's worlds are poor and the mixed ones rich and mortal: births must match deaths, so how eagerly agents breed sets a world's size, and its riches and health with it; the rules tried to hold a world rich and steady, and what is left to try.

chapters.title: Meta XII · Rules in company
chapters.note: What the book's rules do together rather than alone (batches Y, W, X, T, U and V): many rules change sign or size in company; revolutions and gifts are details in B2, handover and lapsing links reshape the network everywhere, the rules of birth set a world's size; evolution goes on in nearly every combination on B2, and no switch makes it go on in B1; and the worlds that are spaces pay for the room with poverty, flatness or cuts.
